title: New Beginnings
author: William Saville
content:
The wind blew westward, and the sky lightened, casting a soft glow over the path ahead. He paused, staring down the road. Though he knew he couldn’t go back to the life he’d left behind, uncertainty gnawed at him. What lay ahead was unknown, but the place he had once called home had become a prison. He reached up to his neck, feeling the cold, silver amulet pressed against his chest; its weight a constant reminder of everything he'd lost. He sighed, resigned to his fate, and pressed forward. The sun rose higher, and the biting early spring wind stung his face. He could only hope that wherever this road led, it would be kinder than what he had fled.

His supplies were nearly gone. The bread he had packed was stale, his water nearly depleted, and he feared for his survival. His cloak, though made for winter, still gave him some comfort as he slept fitfully, the cold gnawing at him and his stomach growling with hunger. Once from a noble family, he had been raised to fit a role; one he had never wanted. Dresses, suitors, and the endless expectations of being someone he wasn't. For years, he had longed to join his brother on hunts and fishing trips, to wear trousers and live freely. But his rebellion had only led to rejection. Just three months prior, he had begun binding his chest and dressing in his brother's clothes, passing himself off as a traveler.

His freedom had been brief. The pretty lass who sold butter and eggs in the market had noticed him, and after weeks of playful flirting, he had stolen a kiss. It was she who had uncovered his secret, when his bound chest brushed against hers. Her shock had led to her father’s fury, and soon, he was dragged before his own father; the town’s mayor. Whipped and punished, he was told if he wanted to be a man, he would be punished as one. He was confined to the servants' quarters, forced to wear dresses once more, and then, after the girl’s father demanded he be removed from the town, his servants helped him escape. Bruised and broken, he fled with only what little he could carry, leaving behind everything he'd ever known.

He awoke in a small, unfamiliar hut, covered in sweat. A girl, her face kind yet firm, was holding a flask of ale to his lips. He sputtered, coughing, unaccustomed to the taste, as she stroked his forehead.

"I'm Malja," she said firmly. "I found you beneath a tree, feverish, and brought you here with my cart. My parents will be home soon from the market. We've been caring for you for three days, sir."

She smiled at him, her eyes warm. "We changed your breast wrap; it was filthy! But don’t worry, we have people like you in our town. You’re safe here. In fact, there's a wizard, Dericka, who was born a man. She helps people like you become who they truly are. She doesn’t charge, because it’s not your fault your body isn’t right. I was born wrong too. I’ve been a girl for seven harvests now. Relax. You're safe here."

His heart tightened at her words, but he nodded slowly.

"What’s your name, sir?"

"I haven’t chosen one yet," he murmured, glancing at the floor. "I was born Taliah, but that name doesn’t fit who I am. It’s dead to me."

Malja cocked her head, a playful smile tugging at her lips. "You look like a Tommin," she teased, "or a Ranlo."

"Ranlo… I like that," he said, the name resonating deep within him. But as he smiled, a coughing fit took over, and Malja quickly hushed him, pressing a cool cloth to his forehead.

He drifted into unconsciousness once more.

When he awoke again, the fire crackled softly, and he could smell something delicious simmering. Malja sat by the fire with an older woman, who was stirring a pot, and a man who was whittling something small and intricate.

"Helena, our guest is awake!" the man boomed, making Ranlo wince at the noise.

"My apologies, sir," the man lowered his voice, clearly noticing Ranlo's discomfort. "My daughter tells me we are to address you as Ranlo?"

"Yes," Ranlo stammered, his face lighting up despite the pounding in his head. "I am Ranlo."

"I’m Fandin," the man said warmly. "You already know my wife and daughter. Welcome to the town of St. Dericka, named after the wizard who founded this place as a haven. We’ve lived here seven harvests since our own town; Boherin; cast us out."

Ranlo’s eyes widened. "Boherin! That’s where I’m from! My father is the mayor!"

He recounted his story; the pain of rejection, the brutal punishment, and how he had come to be here. By the end, both Helena and Malja were in tears.

"Oh, Ranlo," Helena sobbed, embracing him tightly. "You poor dear. You are welcome here. You have a home with us, as long as you need."

Ranlo was overwhelmed by the warmth of her hug. He had never been held like this before. His own mother had never once shown him such affection.

When Helena pulled away, she hurried to the boiling pot, and Malja quickly served everyone. The meal was delicious; something Ranlo had never had, even in his former life of wealth and privilege. There had always been rules about food, about keeping his figure “slender.”

As they ate, they spoke of the town; of the people who had found refuge there, all seeking something different, yet united by love and acceptance. They traded, helped each other, and found peace. Ranlo felt a spark of hope he had not known in years.

"When your fever is gone," Fandin said, smiling kindly, "we’ll take you to Dericka. She’ll help you, and after that, we’ll teach you about farming and caring for animals. How does that sound to you, son?"

"That sounds amazing," Ranlo said, his voice full of excitement. The fever seemed to be breaking, and his color was already improving.

"Let's get you into the bath, Ranlo," Helena said gently. "We must scrub the fever from your skin. Malja, please put the food away and wash the dishes."

Malja nodded and helped her mother.

Helena led Ranlo to the washroom, helping him undress and remove his bindings. He instinctively covered his chest, but Helena reassured him.

"Don’t worry, Ranlo," she said softly. "You won’t have those much longer. Until then, don’t hide from us. We need to scrub every inch of your skin to keep the fever from returning."

He sank into the hot water, and she scrubbed him tenderly, taking care to ensure his body was clean. Ranlo had never felt so loved, so cared for. He knew, deep in his heart, that this was his new home.

"Thank you, Mama," he whispered, tears welling up in his eyes. Helena’s eyes softened, and she embraced him tightly, even though he was still dripping wet.

When the sun rose the next morning, the four of them went to the town square. Dericka, the wizard, was reading to children by the fountain. The moment she saw Ranlo, she smiled knowingly.

"I have seen your heart, young man," Dericka said, her voice warm and compassionate. "I will help you. But tell me, why do you still wear the silver amulet your mother gave you? She didn’t love you as the woman beside you does. In all your fourteen harvests, she never showed you affection, and yet you still wear it."

Ranlo’s eyes burned with emotion as he replied, "I keep it as a reminder never to return to that place. My mother’s love was as cold as this amulet." He paused, swallowing hard. "I planned to sell it for food, but my sister found me before I could." He pulled the amulet from his chest and offered it to Dericka. "I no longer need this reminder of her. Please, take it as payment for what you’re about to do for me."

Dericka smiled, her eyes knowing. "I already knew what you would say. But this amulet is not payment for what I’ve already done for you. Look at your body."

Ranlo glanced down and gasped. His chest was flat, his bindings were loose, and his body had grown taller. He looked like a man.

Dericka handed him a mirror, and he saw his face had changed, too. His features now resembled those of Fandin and Helena.

"Your body has taken the shape you desired," Dericka said. "You wanted to be their son, and so you are. The amulet will be melted into something useful for the town, but it is no longer needed."

Tears welled up in Ranlo’s eyes as he held the mirror to his face.

"Welcome home, Ranlo," Dericka said, smiling warmly. "Welcome home."
